title: When does the bus arrive, and will the door fit?
description: A bus message says four point five hours after noon, and a door is ordered two point five feet wide for an opening of two feet five inches. Each decimal part is changed into minutes or inches before the answer is read. The close ties it to real life.
teaching_notes: One idea: a decimal part of an hour or a foot is tenths of that unit, so change the tenths to minutes or inches. Watch for students who read the digit after the point as minutes or inches.

source: A message says the bus reaches at 4.5 hours post noon. When
video_script.why: The child can read tenths of a unit and now changes them to minutes and inches in two everyday cases.
video_script.substitution: Find what part of the unit the decimal is, then change that part into minutes or inches and read the answer.
video_script.anchor: A bus message that gives the arrival time as a decimal, and a door ordered by a decimal width.
video_script.payoff_line: Change the part after the point into minutes or inches

final_answer.value: 4:30 p.m.; the door was 2 ft 6 inches, 1 inch too wide
final_answer.spoken: half past four in the afternoon; the door was two feet six inches, one inch too wide

names.{{NAME_8}}: gets a message about the time the bus reaches

hold_back: 4:30 p.m.; the door was 2 ft 6 inches, 1 inch too wide
maths_rules: 0.5 hour is 5 parts of 10 equal parts of an hour, and each part is 60 / 10 = 6 minutes
5 x 6 = 30 minutes, so 4.5 hours after noon is 4 hours 30 minutes after noon, which is 4:30 p.m.
1 foot = 12 inches, so 0.5 ft is half of 12 inches, which is 6 inches
2.5 ft = 2 ft 6 inches, and 6 inches is more than 5 inches, so the door is 1 inch too wide for the opening of 2 ft 5 inches
video_script.design: A clock face for one hour is cut into ten equal parts of six minutes, and a foot rule is cut into twelve inches. The five parts are counted off on the clock and the half foot on the rule. The door is then set against the opening to show the extra inch.
